summary: Describes ingress traffic filtering, a simple method to stop denial of service attacks that use forged source IP addresses from spreading out of behind an ISP's aggregation point. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2827 recommends checking the source address of packets as they leave a customer network. Providers can drop packets whose addresses do not belong to that network, reducing attacks that rely on forged addresses. The filter cannot stop a sender from forging an address inside the permitted range.

subtitle: How network providers can stop packets with forged source addresses at the network edge.

tldr.problem: Denial-of-service attacks can use forged source IP addresses to hide their origin and direct replies at unrelated systems.
tldr.mechanism: A provider checks packets arriving from a customer network and forwards only those whose source addresses fall within the prefixes advertised for that network.
tldr.outcome: The filter blocks forged addresses outside the permitted prefixes and can make an attack easier to trace, but it does not stop spoofing within an allowed prefix. RFC 2827 obsoletes RFC 2267 and is updated by RFC 3704.

today: RFC 2827 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 38). It obsoletes RFC 2267 and has been updated by RFC 3704.

sections.title: The Source-Address Spoofing Problem
sections.content:
Denial-of-service attacks can put a false source IP address on packets. This can conceal the sender, consume resources at the target, and cause replies to go to an uninvolved system. RFC 2827 urges providers to filter traffic from downstream networks so that packets claim only addresses within legitimately advertised prefixes.

The proposed filtering does not prevent flooding from valid prefixes. It restricts an attacker inside a network from using forged addresses outside the prefixes allowed for that network. Because remaining packets must use valid, reachable addresses, this can also make their origin easier to trace.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker can put someone else's address on a packet to hide where it came from. This RFC asks providers to reject packets whose source addresses do not belong to the network sending them.

sections.title: How Forged Packets Cause Harm
sections.content:
In the RFC's TCP SYN flood example, an attacker sends connection requests with changing source addresses. A target sends replies to those addresses and waits for connections, using resources even when the addresses cannot be reached. If the attacker uses a real address belonging to another network, that innocent system receives the replies and may be blocked by the target's administrator.

The memo also discusses UDP and ICMP flooding. It recommends restricting UDP diagnostic traffic from outside an administrative domain and not forwarding directed broadcasts by default. The attacks can severely reduce performance or crash a system.
sections.plainLanguage: False source addresses can make a target wait for replies that never come or send replies to an innocent party. Both systems can be harmed, while the attacker is harder to identify.

sections.title: Filtering at the Provider Edge
sections.content:
The provider restricts traffic entering from a downstream network to that network's known, advertised prefixes. In the RFC's example, an ingress filter on router 2 allows packets with a source address within 204.69.207.0/24 and denies packets with any other source address.

Administrators should log dropped packets to help monitor suspicious activity. More generally, an ISP aggregating announcements for several downstream networks should filter traffic that claims to come from outside those announcements.
sections.plainLanguage: A provider checks a packet as it enters from a customer network. It forwards packets with an allowed source address and drops packets claiming to come from elsewhere.

sections.title: Remote Access and Return-Path Checks
sections.content:
The RFC suggests that remote access servers could filter packets from individual users against the address assigned by the provider. It notes that the server would need an option for customers who legitimately connect a network through a remote router.

The authors considered checking whether the return route to a packet's source uses the same interface on which the packet arrived. They rejected this approach because Internet routes are often asymmetric, so the return path may use another interface.
sections.plainLanguage: A remote access server could check that a user's packets use the address assigned to that user. A check based on the return route was rejected because routes may be different in each direction.

sections.title: Special Cases and Limits
sections.content:
Filtering may disrupt special services. Mobile IP is affected because traffic to a mobile node is tunneled while traffic from it may use a source address that does not match the attached network. The RFC describes reverse tunneling, which sends the mobile node's traffic through its home agent before it reaches the Internet.

An attacker can still forge an address belonging to a permitted prefix. Filtering narrows the likely origin to the advertised networks, helping an administrator trace the source or block an address range. Where DHCP or BOOTP is used, administrators should allow appropriate packets from 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255 to reach a relay agent and control directed broadcast forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: Some legitimate traffic, including traffic from a mobile node, may use an address outside the attached network's range. Reverse tunneling can send that traffic through the home agent first. Filtering also cannot stop forged addresses that fall inside an allowed range.

sections.title: Who Should Filter
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that service providers filter at the edges of Internet-connected networks and that corporate administrators filter their own networks. Filtering can reduce the effectiveness of denial-of-service attacks based on forged source addresses and can help locate an attack's origin.

Administrators are responsible for ensuring that their networks do not become the source of this kind of attack. The memo's security discussion says that broader filtering reduces opportunities to use forged source addresses and makes the remaining attacks easier to trace.
sections.plainLanguage: Providers and organizations should check outgoing packets at their network edges. This reduces opportunities to send attacks with false source addresses and can help identify where an attack began.

viz.caption: FILTER RULE FROM THE RFC'S EXAMPLE

data.title: Ingress filter
data.code:
IF packet source is within 204.69.207.0/24
THEN forward as appropriate

IF packet source is anything else
THEN deny packet
